newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish coalition plan boosted by resignation.
newsitem.headline: Turkish coalition plan boosted by resignation.

text.p: Turkish secularist Mesut Yilmaz's bid to form an anti-Islamist coalition was helped on Wednesday by the resignation of a rival right-wing MP, but he still faced a struggle to win enough parliamentary support for his plan.
Deputy Hasan Denizkurdu announced his resignation from conservative leader Tansu Ciller's True Path Party in a four-page letter to the speaker's office.
"I am resigning from the party today to avoid going through a disciplinary process similar to the inquisition courts," his resignation statement said.

Denizkurdu was facing party disciplinary action for refusing to oppose Yilmaz's bid to form a secularist government in place of the Islamist-led coalition which collapsed last week under pressure from the military.
"The coalition put a strain on the country before even completing its first year in office and the basic principles of the republic have become open to question," Denizkurdu said.
Despite the resignation, True Path officials said Ciller had gained assurances from a large majority of her MPs that they would not vote for Yilmaz's proposed coalition.

True Path deputy leader Cihan Pacaci told Reuters only two MPs from the party had failed to put their names to a petition aimed at showing there was majority opposition in parliament to a secularist alliance.
At a news conference, Yilmaz said he was confident he would be able to win clear parliamentary support and cast doubt on True Path unity against him.

"The government that I will form will win a confidence vote and it will not be a matter of winning by a hair's breadth," he told reporters. "We will see about those who signed the petition in the days ahead."
Yilmaz has won the backing of secularist MPs from the left and right but needs the support of around a dozen True Path deputies to win a vote of confidence in the 550-member parliament.
He has given himself until early next week to present President Suleyman Demirel a government list to replace the one-year-old government under Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.
Erbakan resigned to resolve a growing dispute with the military over religious activism. He had proposed the formation of a revamped coalition including his Islamists under Ciller's leadership.

A bitter feud between Motherland Party leader Yilmaz and rival conservative leader Ciller is the main obstacle in the way of a secularist alliance. The two met on Tuesday for 20 minutes of talks where Ciller rejected an offer to support Yilmaz.
He said on Wednesday he would not meet Ciller again in the search for a coalition unless his opponent recognises him as prime minister-designate.
"It is impossible for me to meet Mrs Ciller if she does not change her attitude," Yilmaz said.

Ciller, the caretaker deputy prime minister, says Demirel should have named her instead of Yilmaz. A renewed coalition of True Path and the Islam-based Welfare Party, backed by a far-right party would have the support of 281 deputies on paper.
The Turkish stock market, buffeted in the last two days by speculation over the prospects for such a coalition, drifted lower on Wednesday.
The main market index ended the morning session down 0.3 percent in quiet trading.
